articles.title: Once near extinction, these giant tortoises now outnumber people in the Seychelles, survey finds
articles.summary: Giant tortoises once pushed to the brink of extinction now outnumber humans in their home of the Seychelles, according to a new survey on one of the African nation’s most remote islands.
articles.body: Giant tortoises once pushed to the brink of extinction now outnumber humans in their home of the Seychelles, according to a new survey on one of the African nation’s most remote islands. The survey, led by the Seychelles Islands Foundation (SIF) and the University of Exeter in the UK, estimated that about 180,000 Aldabra giant tortoises live on Aldabra Atoll, an Indian Ocean island group off the east coast of mainland Africa. It is the highest figure ever recorded for the species, and far exceeds the human population of around 122,000 living in the tiny archipelago nation. Aldabra Atoll is one of only two places in the world where giant tortoises are found in the wild. A much smaller population lives on Ecuador’s Galápagos Islands. One of the world’s most undisturbed island ecosystems, Aldabra Atoll is home to several unique species that thrive in the remote haven. The species has rebounded from a dramatic decline. Heavy exploitation during the 19th century reduced its population on the island to fewer than 1,000, pushing the species to the brink of extinction. A recovery program helped secure strict nature reserve status for the atoll in 1981. It became a UNESCO World Heritage site a year later, giving the population room to rebound. “More than 180,000 giant tortoises roaming freely on our atoll is proof of what long-term commitment to conservation can achieve,” Frauke Fleischer-Dogley, CEO of SIF, said in a statement. “This is wonderful news for Seychelles, for the world, and for everyone who has worked to protect Aldabra.” Creating the new estimate required more than just a headcount. The figures are based on an analysis of five years of tortoise counts conducted between 2018 and 2022, and is the first update since a widely cited estimate of 100,000 tortoises in the late 1990s. “Aldabra’s giant tortoise monitoring program is one of the longest running in the region, but the atoll’s dense vegetation makes counting tortoises genuinely difficult in places,” said Nancy Bunbury, one of the study’s co-authors. Bunbury added the team of scientists on the study have produced the most reliable baseline for the species, which can be used as a benchmark to track its population for decades to come. Despite the encouraging population estimate, the study’s authors said continued vigilance is crucial as the climate crisis brings longer and more frequent droughts that could reduce shade and food for the tortoises. Rising sea levels as the planet warms also threaten the atoll’s low-lying habitat. The world’s oldest known tortoise, a 194-year-old called Jonathan, is likely to have come from the Aldabra Atoll or the Granitic Seychelles. Guinness World Records lists Jonathan as the oldest living land animal and the oldest tortoise ever. He was believed to be about 50 years old when he was moved to the British Overseas Territory of St. Helena in 1882.

articles.title: Taliban firmly in control in Afghanistan 25 years after U.S.-led invasion to oust them
articles.summary: Although not quite as extreme as when they previously ruled from 1996 to 2001, the hard-line Islamist regime has reinstated many restrictions, especially on women and girls.
articles.body: KABUL, Afghanistan — Dr. Nigar Nangrahari was on a night shift in a Kabul hospital when the U.S.-led invasion of Afghanistan began 25 years ago — an event that would shape her and her country’s future for decades to come. As she walked home the next morning, Nangrahari saw Kabul residents taking revenge on members of the Taliban, whose harsh, repressive rule had seen public stonings, limb amputations of alleged criminals and women obliterated from public life. “Along the way, I saw ordinary people killing anyone they caught who was a Taliban member. I witnessed with my own eyes the people of Kabul capturing and killing Taliban fighters. Some had climbed trees to hide,” she said. Afraid of what was to come, Nangrahari and her family stayed home for about a month. Eventually, she was called back to the hospital and returned to work as an obstetrician-gynecologist. She no longer had to wear a burqa in the street. “They granted us freedom — but not the kind that Afghans could truly benefit from,” said Nangrahari, 58. Afghanistan is a deeply conservative Muslim society, and the U.S. culture that came with the American presence in the country often rankled some segments of society. “Afghans should neither be completely unrestricted nor subjected to the kind of severe constraints imposed by the Taliban,” she said. “There needs to be a moderate balance.” A bitter legacy Under U.S. President George W. Bush, the American-led coalition launched Operation Enduring Freedom with the stated goal of dismantling Al Qaeda, the terrorist organization whose leader, Osama bin Laden, had orchestrated the Sept. 11 attacks in the United States from his base in Afghanistan. The invasion was to mark the start of a 20-year war that cost tens of thousands of Afghan lives, along with thousands of coalition service members, U.S. contractors, aid workers and journalists. The legacy of that war, and of the successive U.S.-supported Afghan governments during that time, endures today. “Their stated goals were to bring good governance to Afghanistan and to combat narcotics and terrorism,” said Muin Gul Chamkanai, a former doctor who now heads a humanitarian organization, the Shkula Charitable Foundation, and also works as a political analyst. “The reality turned out to be the exact opposite.” At a massive cost, both financial and in lives, the American presence brought certain freedoms, particularly for the media and in women’s education and employment opportunities. But pervasive corruption and often heavy-handed military tactics soon bred deep resentment. Sitting at home on Oct. 7, 2001, Chamkanai switched on his television. The sight of his country being invaded enraged him. “Had I been struck by their bombs, I would have considered martyrdom far preferable. I was not afraid,” he said. “I wanted to fight against them in Afghanistan using both the pen and the gun.” The return of the Taliban Now, 25 years after the invasion and five years after the chaotic U.S. withdrawal from the country, the Taliban are firmly back in control of Afghanistan. Although not quite as extreme as their previous government, when they ruled the country from 1996 to 2001, they have reinstated many draconian restrictions, particularly on women and girls. Security has improved without question since the Taliban seized power in August 2021. Gone are the endless devastating bombings and attacks, the vast majority of them carried out by the Taliban themselves during the two-decade-long war. “After a long and arduous struggle, jihad and great sacrifices, Afghans succeeded in liberating their country,” deputy government spokesman Hamdullah Fitrat said in a statement on the 25th anniversary of the invasion. “This struggle demonstrated that Afghans will never submit to foreign occupation or external coercion.” He said that Oct. 7, 2001, was “a dark day in the country’s history that resulted in thousands of Afghans being martyred, wounded, imprisoned, displaced and left homeless.” But for a generation who grew up under U.S.-supported governments, the loss of personal freedoms, especially for women, who face restrictions on everything from what they wear to where they can go, has been a brutal blow. After the Taliban took over, “gradually … restrictions were imposed, and the normal life we had known was taken away. Things became very difficult for us,” said Tahmina Mangal, a 33-year-old woman who saw her hopes of continuing her studies dashed by the shuttering of high schools and universities for girls and women. “The burden is immense. It weighs heavily on my own spirits and psyche,” she said. A perilous future Now, Tahmina owns and runs a store selling traditional Afghan clothing for women. Although women face multiple restrictions and are barred from most jobs, the Ministry of Commerce does issue business licenses to women, she said. She viewed that as the only avenue open to her. But with women barred from education and participation in any form of governance, she worries deeply about the future. “If this situation persists, Afghanistan’s future is perilous,” Tahmina said. “Without women pursuing their studies or receiving an education, we will lack doctors, teachers and literate women, including mothers capable of raising healthy children for society. I view Afghanistan’s future as bleak and dire if this trend continues.” For Nangrahari, although the Taliban government’s emphasis on improving infrastructure in the country is welcome, its emphasis on religious education for boys, and its ban on higher education for girls, “sets Afghanistan back by a century.” Afghanistan already is among the world’s poorest countries. “Roads have been improved and high-rise buildings constructed. Indeed, infrastructure is the foundation of the economy, and we acknowledge all of this,” Nangrahari said. “But a society lacking education is zero.” Still, sitting in her clothing shop in Kabul, Tahmina said that women shouldn’t give up hope, and should continue pursuing their studies, even if it is only online. “Governments inevitably come and go, collapses happen, and no government lasts forever,” she said. “I always say: ‘Remain hopeful for the future. Study, pursue professional training alongside your regular schooling, and seek higher education.’”

articles.title: Mexico prison clash in strife-torn Sinaloa state leaves 10 dead
articles.summary: Nine inmates and one visitor killed in Sinaloa prison riot, local authorities say.
articles.body:
Ten people have been killed and 16 others injured in a fight at the El Castillo Penitentiary Centre in the city of Mazatlan, in Mexico’s northwestern state of Sinaloa, state authorities said.

The Sinaloa Public Security Secretariat said on Thursday that a fight inside the prison had left nine inmates and a family visitor dead.

Sinaloa’s Secretary of Public Security, Sinuhe Tellez, said in a video posted on social media that the visitor was a minor.

The 16 injured inmates were transferred for medical attention, the secretariat said.

An inter-institutional group of security forces moved in, and the prison is now “under control”, with authorities remaining at the site, the secretariat added.

Social work staff are contacting the families of the dead, Tellez said, noting that visits to the prison had been suspended as a precaution and the rest of the prison population was safe.

Sinaloa is a battleground for warring factions of the Sinaloa drug cartel and is one of six Mexican states the US State Department advises Americans not to visit over security concerns.

Officials have not said whether the violence at the prison was linked to that conflict.

articles.title: Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work?
articles.summary: The price of fuel has soared as the cost of living emerges as a key issue for millions of Americans.
articles.body:
Prices for gasoline and diesel have more than doubled since the US-Israel conflict with Iran began in February, affecting transport businesses, farmers and anyone who drives a vehicle in America.

Ahead of the critical midterm elections, there have been growing calls for more to be done to reduce the price of fuel, and US President Donald Trump has made several comments and announcements aimed at getting costs down.

The question is: what is he able to do with just a few weeks to go before election day - and will it work?

Why does Trump want to reduce gas and diesel prices?

Trump's announcement of a waiver on the use of red dye diesel at a campaign stop this week underscored the importance of gas prices in a midterm election dominated by affordability issues.

The election comes as there is widespread public concern over the rising costs of fuel, food and other goods. Voters have tied the issue to Trump and his party, weighing down Republicans running in November.

Polls show a majority of Americans disapprove of Trump's handling of the economy and the war in Iran, which has contributed to high diesel and gas prices in the US.

Global oil supplies have been restricted since the conflict in the Middle East effectively halted the usual flow of oil and refined products through the Strait of Hormuz for months.

While the flow of crude oil is nearly back to pre-war levels the price remains above $100 a barrel, and sustained high oil prices have had a knock-on effect for diesel and gasoline.

David Ruisard, pricing manager for commodities intelligence firm Argus says the ongoing Russian war with Ukraine has also impacted oil supplies, contributing to higher fuel prices.

"Our estimates are that your price increase from about $3 a gallon up to $6 a gallon [for diesel] is 60% connected to the Strait of Hormuz, 40% connected to the Russia-Ukraine conflict," he says.

Those higher energy prices are responsible for most of the uptick in inflation this year, Oxford Economics chief US economist Michael Pearce says, which is pushing up interest rates.

"The combined impact of higher rates and higher energy prices is squeezing household budgets and adding to firms' costs," he says.

While prices remain high, Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis for fuel price tracking website GasBuddy said there have been modest declines recently for both gasoline and diesel.

"A lot of that is likely due to some of the manoeuvres that we've seen the Trump administration employ over the last couple of weeks," he said.

The president announced this week that he would allow so-called red dye diesel - fuel which is used off-road and does not face federal taxes - to be used on US highways without facing federal levies.

Ruisard said the only difference in the diesel used by truck drivers and everyday consumers and the tax-free red dye diesel is the dye itself.

"The problem with that red dye is, it's extremely hard to clean it out of your tank," he explained.

The problem that creates is what happens to trucking companies that use the dyed diesel once the temporary tax relief ends, he said.

"The fines are pretty high for having that in your fuel tank because its considered tax evasion."

The other issue with expanding the use of red dye diesel, according to Ruisard, is that people and businesses - including rail operators - usually set aside a particular amount of the product.

"If suddenly people go out and they start consuming that diesel, that depletes their available supply as well," he said.

But another move from Trump has been more successful, according to analysts.

Last week, the G7 countries announced they would release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from stockpiles to ease supply concerns , following pressure from Trump to do so.

De Haan says the announcement itself – regardless of how much has been released so far – "has worked to push prices down to some degree".

Economist Pearce agreed but warned the release is only a temporary solution.

"As long as energy exports from the Gulf remain disrupted, stocks will need to be drained further to supply the market," he said. "And the need to refill those stocks will mean energy prices remain elevated for a period, even when disruption in the Middle East clears."

Earlier this week, Trump said he was "thinking about" suspending federal tax on gasoline.

De Haan said the president has also been imploring states to cut state taxes on gasoline and several have done so, including Ohio and Georgia.

State taxes form a "moderate portion" of what consumers pay at the pump, and those reductions have helped reduce prices and national averages, he said.

However, suspending or reducing the federal levy on gasoline would require the cooperation of Congress.

"That may be difficult to obtain ahead of the midterm elections," said De Haan.

De Haan estimated that in Indiana, which cut its tax on gasoline in May, it has cost the state government $1bn (£760m) in lost revenue.

Trump has also previously supported calls for a ban on diesel exports from the US.

While that would provide partial relief in the Gulf and Midwest, according to Pearce, he adds it would be of "little benefit" to the Northeast and West Coast.

"The policy risks backfiring because it would result in stockpiling of diesel, and as that storage runs out, refineries would need to cut back on production," he said.

"That would raise prices of other energy products, including gasoline."

Does Trump have any other levers to pull?

De Haan believes the president has "basically pulled all of the small levers that a president can pull, and we're still seeing prices very elevated".

"The only way out of this to reduce gas prices in a meaningful way is solve one or both of the geopolitical tensions that are causing high prices," he said.

That means reaching a deal with Iran and helping facilitate an agreement between Ukraine and Russia - which, Pearce said, are issues that cannot be directly controlled by the White House.

Even if those conflicts are resolved, Ruisard said that due to damage to facilities in the Middle East caused by military strikes it would still take production four to six months to return to normal.

"The message to consumers and industry is that regardless of what happens and whether the president is able to successfully negotiate that kind of a deal," he said.

"High prices are here to stay for a little while at least."

articles.title: Hand-built £85k electric sports car set to be made in Nuneaton
articles.summary: Car maker Longbow, which hopes to build thousands of cars, says the region has the talent and know-how.
articles.body:
A British carmaker has unveiled plans to start production of its hand-built electric sports car in Warwickshire.

Longbow is to start production of its limited-edition Speedster at Mira Tech Park in Nuneaton next year.

West Midlands mayor Richard Parker, who backed Longbow with £3m from a government fund, said the project will be followed by the firm's Roadster model, creating more than 200 skilled jobs.

Daniel Davey, Longbow's co-chief executive officer, said the region was the best place to build the cars. "It's not just the supply chain; you've got the talent here and the know-how," he said.

Davey said: "You cannot build this car anywhere else in the world. And if you did, you would be importing UK components to it.

"So you can get heavy components elsewhere, and you can get high-volume components elsewhere; what we're looking for is low-volume, high-quality, low-cost, low-weight."

The Speedster has a waiting list of prospective buyers from across the world, waiting to spend around £85,000 on the sports car.

At the test track at Mira, the all-British creation silently demonstrated how a lightweight sports car can go from an idea to a vehicle in less than two years, helped by regional expertise.

Longbow said the UK was good at building lightweight sports cars.

"Our designers are just up the road in Leamington Spa, engineers from across the West Midlands and further afield," Davey added.

The project was backed by £3m from the government's £50m West Midlands Supplier Readiness and Transformation fund , which aims to accelerate the UK's transition to electric vehicle (EV) manufacturing.

Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said the £3m was to strengthen the supply chain and the industry.

West Midlands Combined Authority said the money would be match-funded by Longbow, which plans to manufacture more than 10,000 cars a year.

Parker said: "We've been building cars here in West Midlands for 130 years, so what better location for a new generation of carmakers like Longbow.

"They know this industry inside out and are investing here because this is quite simply the best place in the UK to build a car."

Car industry expert Professor David Bailey said: "They're trying to do what Tesla first did many years ago with a sort of lightweight, fast electric sports car.

"So I think it's great; it shows we have great research and development skills. We can probably compete, I think, in terms of low-volume, high-margin cars, but more broadly we need to be doing a lot more to support the auto industry in the region and enable it to continue growing."

articles.title: The Music Man Project fulfills late MP Sir David Amess's dream
articles.summary: The Music Man Project is a charity in Essex that teaches music to people with learning disabilities.
articles.body:
A music group with learning disabilities received a standing ovation as they fulfilled a dream of the late MP Sir David Amess.

The Music Man Project is a charity based in Southend-on-Sea, Essex, that teaches children and adults with learning disabilities to sing, sign and play original music.

They have performed for the King, at the Royal Albert Hall and London Palladium, but a trip to perform in New York was the dream of their former president and Southend West MP Amess before he was murdered in 2021.

The project's founder David Stanley said: "Following his death, I just made it my mission to fulfil that promise, really, in his memory."

"So that we remember Sir David for all of the work he did for championing people with learning disabilities in Southend, and then obviously across the country, through the Music Man Project's expansion."

Stanley, who wrote, produced and featured in the show, paid a tribute to Amess during the performance.

With a crack in his voice, he spoke into a megaphone - one of Amess' signature accessories on the political campaign trail - the words: "We promised we'd get them to the Broadway and we did it my friend, we did it."

The morning after, Stanley told the BBC he was "exhausted" and "overwhelmed with emotion".

"We got a brilliant standing ovation," he said.

"It's nothing short of what the students deserved.

"To be fair though, they've got a standing ovation from the King at the Royal Albert Hall before, so this was expected really with something like this."

They performed at the Town Hall in New York with a full house of almost 1,500 people, and a venue known for its historic significance.

It was founded in 1921 by suffragists and one of the only venues in New York to openly welcome Black artists.

Stanley said his group were "perfect" and "incredible" on the night.

He said it proved what he has always said about people with learning difficulties.

"We give them the opportunities and you believe in them and you have high expectations of what they can achieve, then they will always come through, they surprise you.

"Decades ago we would have hidden certain parts of society away, now they're performing on Broadway."

Their performance told the story of the group's journey, from its beginnings 27 years ago to where they are now with 200 members.

Stanley told BBC Essex presenter Sonia Watson that their visit would also include a performance at the United Nations.

"I get to make a speech at the UN. So it's full of pinch me moments this tour."

articles.title: Sustainable fashion project in West secures £850k funding
articles.summary: The initiative will involve year-round clothing swaps, repair cafes and upcycling workshops.
articles.body:
A four-year project aimed at inspiring climate action through sustainable fashion has secured funding of almost £850k.

It will fund high street hubs across the country offering repair workshops, clothing swaps and skill-sharing opportunities as well as research into behaviours around sustainable fashion.

Bath Spa University and Bristol-based community interest company A Single Thread have launched the initiative Restitch the Future after getting funding from the National Lottery's Community Action Fund.

Amelia Twine, founder of A Single Thread CIC, said, "too often sustainable fashion is perceived as expensive, exclusive or unrealistic" but the initiative is about "changing that narrative".

Bath Spa University says fashion is responsible for up to 10% of global carbon emissions, often due to sustainable alternatives being thought of as inaccessible, unaffordable or out of reach for many communities.

Bristol care home chef through to UK best finals

Red route 'could make small businesses go extinct'

Residents win Curo service charge legal battle

Twine, from Bristol, said: "Fashion is one of the most urgent but often overlooked climate challenges we face.

"By creating practical opportunities for people to repair, reuse and rethink clothing, we're making sustainable fashion more accessible and empowering people to take meaningful climate action," she added.

The four-year Restitch the Future project aims to build practical skills in community hubs on the high street.

There have already been temporary hubs set up across the country including in Bristol, Bath, Wellington, Stroud and Cheltenham.

But Twine hopes to roll out a number of permanent hubs over the next four years.

The initiative focuses on the consumer and tries to encourage them to "shop differently and to reduce how much fast fashion they buy", which Twine believes is the "quickest way to shift the whole system".

However, as an organisation, A Single Thread is also looking to "lobby the government to bring in different regulations to restrict brands and how they operate," added Twine.

Bath Spa University will be leading the research programme exploring the barriers that prevent people from engaging with sustainable fashion, including affordability and representation.

Last year, it launched its own sustainable fashion initiative, Future Fashion Works, with the aim of connecting students with local creatives and independent designers.

Tamara Parsons-Baker, head of Future Fashion Works, said they wanted to "better understand what enables lasting behaviour change around fashion consumption."

She added that the project will generate "vital evidence while creating meaningful social and environmental impact across the UK".

articles.title: Norwich data centre raises fears of noise and wildlife impact
articles.summary: The data centre, which will have 72 chiller units on its roof, will generate 150 jobs, planners hear.
articles.body:
A huge data centre planned in a village near a nature reserve would generate "very high noise levels" without extensive measures to block it, experts have said.

Plans have been submitted to South Norfolk Council for a 150 megawatt facility in Keswick on the edge of Norwich, which includes assessments of its potential environmental impact.

The scheme is causing concern, with thousands of people signing a petition against it, due to fears it could harm neighbouring wildlife sites.

But Norwich Apex Data Centre has defended the scheme, claiming assessments showed it would not harm protected areas like Marston Marshes.

The data centre is also causing concern over its potential water usage, noise pollution and the scale of the facility harming the landscape.

Assessments of the noise it could create found it has the "potential to generate very high levels of noise to the surrounding area" and would require extensive mitigation measures.

The majority of noise would come from the 72 chiller units on the roof.

A spokesperson said: "Our environmental assessments conclude the data centre will not harm nearby designated wildlife sites.

"The data centre will use air-cooling technology, meaning no water will be required for cooling. Water will only be needed for everyday uses, such as toilets and staff facilities, with none taken from nearby rivers or marshes.

"The facility has also been designed so that operational noise levels at surrounding sensitive locations are in line with existing background levels."

The firm also said the facility could create up to 150 permanent jobs and that it would create planting and landscaping to screen the development and reduce the visual impact.

It would also be located close to an electrical substation for offshore wind farms in the North Sea, from which it could draw power.

The project has already been met with opposition, with thousands signing a petition against it.

Daniel Elmer, the Conservative leader of South Norfolk Council and county councillor for Keswick, said he will formally object to the proposed facility.

He told the Local Democracy Reporting Service: "My personal view, is that it is just too damned big for the site it would be on.

"It is right next to the marshes and the southern edge of Norwich, while it is near a listed church.

"That's the southern gateway into the city of Norwich. I think you have to think, in terms of the Norwich 'brand', what visitors to the city would see when they travel down that road.

"What they see needs to be aesthetically pleasing and I am not sure that is what they will get, given the application which has been submitted at the moment."

articles.title: Woodbridge brass band celebrates 180th anniversary - and romance
articles.summary: Woodbridge Excelsior Band are marking their 180th anniversary.
articles.body:
"In those days it was said that women or girls didn't have enough puff to be able to play a brass instrument, so brass bands were all men."

In 1971, Jackie Walker was only the second woman to join the Woodbridge Excelsior Band in Suffolk.

Although meeting a boyfriend wasn't Jackie's aim, the ratios were in her favour.

"There were several [boys] in the band that used to turn up outside my parents' house in their cars to pick me up on a Tuesday night for band," said Jackie, who grew up in nearby Martlesham.

"Gradually as more girls joined they all liked Andrew.... I was the one that got him."

Andrew had joined a few months before when there were no girls in the band, after responding to an advert.

"It needed to get some new blood in, they were all very elderly gentlemen," he recalled.

The couple married in 1978 and have continued to play together, with Jackie going on to be co-musical director.

"It's the best thing you can do," Andrew said about being in the band.

"You're with your friends, playing good music, going out places, what more do you want out of life?"

As the band prepares for a special concert marking their 180th anniversary, the line-up of musicians looks quite different.

They have 20 men and 12 women, with a mix of ages.

Kayra plays tenor horn, having joined aged eight.

"I think it's such an honour to play and I love telling people about it," the 17-year-old said.

"[The instruments] are all kind of beautiful pieces... I always think it's amazing how basically piping can make such wonderful noises!"

Tilly Crookall, 20, plays cornet and said: "I just love finishing work and then coming here and seeing all my friends and just playing different music."

The band was formed in 1846 as the Woodbridge Temperance Band, changing name to the Excelsior Band in 1916.

In 1969 the band played on the same bill as Deep Purple

Being the first brass band to play at the National Film Theatre (renamed BFI Southbank) in London for the premiere of the film Akenfield in 1974

In 1977 the band was invited to record a TV advert for Golden Wonder Crisps

In 2005 they performed aboard HMS Grafton for the final visit of the vessel to Ipswich as it was being decommissioned

In 2009 they took part in the filming of a children's programme hosted by Richard Hammond called Blast Lab, trying to play so loud that the decibels shattered a glass greenhouse

Tom Morris is co-musical director, alongside Jackie Walker.

He told BBC Radio Suffolk: "People come from different walks of life; a lot of people are retired, a couple of students, people who work full time.

"They come to let off steam, to enjoy the music, to meet their friends, so it's trying to mould all those together as part of an organisation

"We have a completely full band and we actually have extra members now which I don't think has happened many times in the history of the band, so the future is bright and the band's healthy."

The band are performing a free anniversary concert at 14:30 on Sunday at Woodbridge Community Hall.

articles.title: How October 7 changed Lebanon and Hezbollah’s political reality
articles.summary: Analysts say Hezbollah’s decision on October 8 to join a ‘war of support’ for Gaza changed Lebanon’s political reality.
articles.body:
Beirut, Lebanon – A day after the October 7, 2023, attack on Israel and the beginning of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, Hezbollah made the decision to join the war, in what it said was support of the Palestinian people. It is a decision that analysts say has forever shaped Lebanese politics.

Experts said the group had underestimated the depth of Israel’s intelligence penetration in the run-up to the war, which later manifested in the bloody September 2024 pager attack and the assassination of much of Hezbollah’s leadership , including Secretary-General Hassan Nasrallah.

“Hezbollah got sucked into a vortex which culminated in the decapitation of their leadership and the invasion of south Lebanon,” Nicholas Blanford, a non-resident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council and author of a book about Hezbollah, told Al Jazeera. “That dealt Hezbollah a major blow to their popular standing and galvanised the election of Joseph Aoun as president and the formation of a new government that took a much stronger line against [the group].”

Hezbollah’s decisions have left the group politically weakened. And while analysts say the group has not been defeated, despite claims to the contrary from some critics, it is no longer the political or military hegemon in Lebanon it once was.

Before October 7, Hezbollah – a group representing Lebanon’s large Shia community – was the strongest political and military actor inside the country. The Iranian-backed group’s influence stretched across the region. Hezbollah was a key ally of the al-Assad regime in Syria and helped it retake territory from anti-Assad opposition groups. It also had connections with allies in places such as Iraq and Yemen.

Hezbollah had key electoral influence in Lebanon, where it often wielded its power to elect or collapse governments. It was also not against deploying its supporters against movements opposed to it, as in 2019 when they took to the streets of Beirut to beat back protesters calling for political reform of the country’s sectarian system, in which Hezbollah has become a key player in the years since the end of Lebanon’s 15-year civil war in 1990.

In the months leading up to October 2023, Hezbollah’s confidence was on clear display. Blanford pointed to examples such as a military parade in south Lebanon conducted by Hezbollah, and the group erecting tents in the Shebaa Farms – on territory that Lebanon considers occupied by Israel.

At the time, Israel was roiled by protests, and Nasrallah was delivering speeches predicting the imminent doom of Israel. The decision to join the fight against Israel in what became known in Lebanon as the War of Support came on October 8, 2023.

“October 7 set in motion a chain of events that Lebanon’s political system was not properly prepared to manage,” Jad Dilati, a political analyst from Nabatieh in southern Lebanon, told Al Jazeera. “Hezbollah opened its support front for Gaza on October 8 completely unilaterally, without any cabinet decision or governmental consensus or even taking into account the positions of the southern [Lebanese] residents who were most affected and still are most affected by these actions.”

“Hezbollah opened the support front on October 8, genuinely believing that it was operating from a position of strength,” Dilati said. “Most of the South believed that Hezbollah was operating from a position of strength after it had spent years building precision missile capabilities, an elaborate tunnel network and these missiles that we were told can hit every building in Tel Aviv.”

For the next 11 months, Israel and Hezbollah traded attacks, albeit with Israel hitting Lebanon more than five times for every Hezbollah attack. Tens of thousands from southern Lebanon and northern Israel fled their homes.

But in September 2024, Israel unilaterally intensified attacks. The Israeli-induced carnage came quickly and heavily, with nearly 500 people killed on September 23 alone . When Nasrallah was said to have accepted a ceasefire – according to Lebanese officials quoted in media reports – Israel ordered his assassination and the evacuation of areas of Beirut’s southern suburbs .

“When Nasrallah was amenable to a ceasefire, Israel was on the offensive and wasn’t going to return to the previous status quo,” Blanford said.

Israel invaded southern Lebanon in October 2024 and stayed in Lebanese territory for more than two months after a ceasefire was agreed in November. Despite the ceasefire, Israel continued to destroy homes and infrastructure in southern Lebanon and refused to pull its troops out of five locations on Lebanese territory. Next door in Syria, the fall of the al-Assad regime in December 2024 also dealt a blow to the group, as its land routes to receive weapons and funding from Iran were disrupted.

Over the next 14 months, Israel violated the ceasefire more than 10,000 times. Then in March 2026, Israel reintensified its war on Lebanon. The attacks came after Hezbollah fired rockets at Israel for the first time in more than a year as a response to the myriad ceasefire violations and the assassination of Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, whom Hezbollah viewed as a religious and political leader.

Israel then invaded Lebanon again and launched widespread attacks on the country. It has killed more than 9,000 people in Lebanon since 2024 and displaced more than 1.2 million people, emptying entire regions of the country.

Israel now occupies large swathes of Lebanese territory, stretching up to 10 kilometres (more than 6 miles) from the border at some points. Dozens of villages, once filled with agriculture and people, are now uninhabited piles of dust and rubble. Hundreds of thousands remain displaced.

This has had a massive impact on Lebanon. The World Bank says the country’s economy has contracted by more than 6 percent in 2026. After the 2024 conflict, the World Bank said Lebanon needed around $11bn for recovery and reconstruction. That figure is likely much higher now.

In the aftermath of past wars against Israel, such as in 2006, Hezbollah was able to support much of its community and supporters. Providing social welfare has been key to the group’s ability to maintain popularity and belief among its constituents.

But since 2024, the Lebanese state, along with much of the international community, has been working to expand its own services. The state is also openly claiming it is working to disarm Hezbollah, despite the group’s objections, as part of a framework agreement with Israel.

“Hezbollah is in a legitimacy crisis that it has not faced before,” Dilati said. “I wouldn’t say that there is a rupture in the community or a complete political realignment, but a big part of the communities that supported it for decades are saying that Iran left them behind, the war was fought on their land for someone else’s interests, and that they don’t want wars anymore.”

Still, while grumbles against the group are growing louder, analysts said Hezbollah remains the most popular representative among Lebanon’s Shia Muslims.

“Hezbollah is providing for their needs by and large, and there is no alternative politically for the Shia community at the moment,” Blanford said. “What is binding them to Hezbollah is the fact that several hundred thousand Shias were booted out of their homes and are living in non-Shia areas where they do not feel particularly welcome, and this can create a sense of vulnerability that naturally makes them gravitate to Hezbollah as communal protection, rightly or wrongly.”

The group also maintains fighting capacity, and despite critics calling it a spent force, analysts and foreign diplomats say its weakness has been overstated. Much of the group’s future depends on the outcome of regional events, particularly regarding the US-Israeli war on Iran. But analysts said the status quo – in which the state is negotiating with Israel and trying to extend its influence across Lebanese territory, and Hezbollah adapts to waning domestic influence – could work against the group.

“The key thing is this looks like a long occupation, and you may get a situation where people who have not only lost their home but lost their village, orchards, banana plantations, tobacco fields and the rest of it may think life was good before and may start blaming Hezbollah,” Blanford said.

articles.title: One of the world’s wealthiest cities is enduring the world’s most polluted air. Here’s why
articles.summary: Singapore becomes world’s most polluted city from toxic smog in Indonesia
articles.body: Singapore, one of the wealthiest cities in the world, has become the most polluted on the planet as it chokes under a blanket of thick, toxic smog caused by fires in neighboring Indonesia. Pollution has cast a pall on the city-state as it gets ready to host a packed weekend of marquee events ranging from international conferences to the glitzy Formula One Grand Prix night race. Air quality in the city-state was at the “very unhealthy” range with an air quality index (AQI) of 216 Friday mid-morning, according to Swiss air quality monitor IQAir. The financial hub topped the list of most polluted cities by IQAir this week and was still at the top spot Friday morning. Kuala Lumpur, also deeply affected by the Indonesian fires, was at number two. Singapore’s skyline, including Marina Bay Sands and other skyscrapers were reduced to faint silhouettes amid the pollution. The key Asian financial hub – with a population of 6.21 million and annual GDP of more than $650 billion – and neighboring Malaysia have had to endure the haze almost annually. Fires in Indonesia are an annual event during the country’s dry season when huge stretches of peatland are cleared and drained for commercial plantations, including those that produce palm oil, an ingredient used in a slew of products from noodles to toothpaste. But this year, the arrival of what’s expected to be a “super” El Niño — a supercharged version of the natural climate pattern which tends to bring bone dry conditions to the country — has set the stage for unusually intense blazes. In an update on its website Thursday, Singapore’s National Environment Agency said “moderate to dense smoke plumes from southern and central Sumatra and West Kalimantan were observed to drift towards Singapore,” referring to Indonesian regions. “Under the prevailing southeasterly or southerly winds, smoke haze may continue to drift towards Singapore,” it added. Entertainment events held outdoors at the F1 event in Singapore could potentially be affected but not the race itself, the motorsport’s governing FIA said Thursday, according to Reuters. On Friday, race organizer Singapore GP told CNN “there are currently no plans to modify our entertainment activities” at the event. Acts to entertain F1 spectators include Janet Jackson and The Killers, among others. This is not the first time the Singapore night race is facing air quality issues. The races in 2015 and 2019 were also enveloped in thick haze and they went ahead. Nevertheless, the Singapore Tourism Board told CNN on Friday: “Action plans are in place based on the intensity of the haze.” F1 drivers, however, don’t seem too bothered. Cadillac driver Valtteri Bottas, who cycled more than 400km (248 miles) from Malaysia to Singapore this week, told Reuters: “I don’t feel like it’s that extreme yet. I mean, it’s not great, but I don’t think there’s that much you can do.” Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton told Reuters he has “much bigger issues to focus on.” Neighboring Malaysia has also been heavily affected by the smog with the education ministry shutting schools across several states this week as the situation worsens.

articles.title: Afghanistan’s emerald miners struggle with tools but attract global buyers
articles.summary: Afghan miners endure harsh conditions, relying on basic tools to extract precious emeralds in Panjshir’s steep valleys.
articles.body:
Panjshir, Afghanistan — At a packed hall in the offices of the Panjshir provincial government, an auction is under way and the bidding is brisk.

The buyers, many from Kabul and some from overseas, have already closely examined the small piles of roughly cut green stones, shining their phone flashlights through them to check their quality.

Bidding for the best stones is competitive.

“Panjshir emeralds have many buyers around the world because of their very high quality,” gem merchant Ghulam Mustafa Habibi told Al Jazeera. “This is why their price is higher compared with other emeralds around the world.”

By the end of the auction, nearly 3,000 carats of the precious stones were sold – the 23rd sale of its kind so far this year. The value of emeralds sold to date in Afghanistan is estimated to be nearly 400m Afghanis ($6.12m), a steep rise compared with last year.

For a country impoverished by years of war and burdened by international sanctions, the trade in precious minerals is a valuable resource, especially in the remote corner of northeastern Afghanistan.

“Thankfully, more than 15,000 people are currently employed in Panjshir’s mining sector,” says Muhammad Aman Rezaii, a mining official responsible for overseeing the operation of many small artisanal mining operations dotting the Panjshir valley.

On the valley’s steep hillsides, miners toil for hours underground to make a living. In the otherwise barren and rocky landscape, which yields little, the precious stones are a lifeline.

“There are hardly any companies or manufacturing factories here. The main source of employment is the mining sector,” said Rezaii, adding that they have identified more than 2,000 other mining sites which could be developed.

Since taking power in 2021, the Taliban say they have signed deals with dozens of investors, mainly Chinese, Russian and Iranian, to mine gemstones and other valuable minerals.

According to the World Bank, state revenues rose 22 percent year-on-year in April and May, boosted by the auction of mines and other resources such as oil and precious minerals.

But Afghanistan’s gemstone mining sector is still lacking in international investment and expertise.

“There have been various proposals to establish an international market for Afghanistan’s precious minerals, particularly in Kabul,” Hafiz Muhammad Agha Hakim, the Governor of Panjshir province, told Al Jazeera.

“Processing machinery could be brought in so that these minerals can be processed and standardised here before being exported to markets around the world. At the moment, there is no standardised centre or proper processing facility.”

Back in the dusty confines of his mine, working in near-total darkness, miner Mahdi wields a crowbar while his friend beside him hits the surface with a hammer. He bemoans their lack of modern equipment.

“There are many challenges because we don’t have advanced equipment,” he says, taking a break from the digging. “We work only with basic tools such as shovels, pickaxes, drills and similar equipment.”

Rezaii said the miners need proper equipment that can make their work easier and safer, while also allowing the minerals to be extracted in a more professional manner. This would benefit the people of Afghanistan and particularly the miners,” he said.

“The area is vulnerable to landslides, avalanches, flooding and falling rocks. People here are working under extremely difficult and demanding conditions.”

articles.title: Who is Dov Lando, the Israeli rabbi criticising Zionism?
articles.summary: The senior rabbi, whose party is in Netanyahu’s coalition, has caused uproar in Israel by calling Zionism disastrous.
articles.body:
One of Israel’s top ultra-Orthodox rabbis, Dov Lando, has become the centre of controversy in Israel after comments emerged in which he denigrated Zionism.

In a recently released video recording, the 96-year-old rabbi is heard saying the ideology of Zionism caused the Jewish people to suffer “disasters”, and that Jewish Israelis may have been better off without a state.

The remarks have drawn rebukes from Israeli politicians weeks before landmark legislative elections, in which the role of the country’s growing ultra-Orthodox community – particularly over military service – is a major issue. The political alignment of ultra-Orthodox parties could also prove crucial to the formation of the next government.

So, who is Lando and why are his comments significant?

Dov Lando is a 96-year-old rabbi regarded as the leader of Israel’s Lithuanian ultra-Orthodox community. Born in Poland and raised in the Lithuanian-style ultra-Orthodox tradition, Lando heads a yeshiva – a traditional Jewish academy – in the Israeli city of Bnei Brak.

He is a member of Moetzes Gedolei HaTorah, a council of senior ultra-Orthodox rabbis that offer religious guidance to the community, as well as the spiritual leader of Israel’s Degel HaTorah party. That party is part of the United Torah Judaism (UTJ) alliance, which is a member of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition.

Earlier this week, Israeli media released a video of Lando making year-old comments that harshly criticise Zionism , military service and secular Israelis.

Lando, who has made similarly critical remarks before, is heard in the video saying that Zionism “caused the Arabs to hate us” and brought physical as well as spiritual “disasters” on the Jewish people.

“It is possible to live well with the Arabs without a state,” Lando said, adding that international or Palestinian rule would have been “the best situation” for Jews.

Lando went on to castigate soldiers who adhere to Religious Zionism – a strand of Orthodox Judaism that upholds Zionism – saying “they are killed because their rabbis teach them a distorted Torah.” Many military operations, he said, are carried out “not for saving lives, but for the honour of the state”.

The veteran rabbi also had harsh words for secular Israelis, who he said have “no connection to Judaism at all”. He described them as having built “a state of apostasy and heresy”.

Lando’s remarks have drawn fierce criticism from numerous Israeli politicians, including all major figures that have joined an opposition alliance challenging Netanyahu.

Gadi Eisenkot, head of the Yashar party who is viewed as the opposition bloc’s most likely candidate for prime minister, said Lando’s “outrageous statements” were “the embodiment of anti-Zionism”.

Yair Lapid, the head of Israel’s opposition in the Knesset, called the comments “a disgrace to every Jew”.

Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, who leads the Together alliance co-founded with Lapid, said Lando’s remarks are “anti-Semitic, anti-Zionist” and against the Israeli military.

Netanyahu has not commented on Lando’s latest reported remarks, but he publicly condemned earlier statements by the rabbi in July, when Lando accused the Religious Zionism movement of “incitement to murder” for its support for drafting religious seminary students into the military.

Could the controversy impact Israel’s upcoming elections?

Members of the anti-Netanyahu opposition bloc have called for the UTJ, which Lando’s party is part of, to be cast out of any future government, and criticised Netanyahu for staying aligned with the group.

Yair Golan, head of the Democrats party, said Netanyahu is “silent because without Rabbi Lando and his emissaries, he has no government”.

Netanyahu’s “political survival is more important to him than Zionism, more than equality in service, and more than the blood of our soldiers”, Golan said.

But breaking with the UTJ would come at a huge political cost to Netanyahu, whose coalition is already in for a tough election battle on October 27 and is polling well below the 61-seat threshold needed for a majority.

UTJ is projected to win 8 seats in parliament, according to an October 5 poll by Israel’s Channel 12.

“If Netanyahu attacks Lando forcefully, he pays a price with the Haredim (ultra-Orthodox) he needs to form a government,” said Ehab Jabareen, a researcher on Israeli affairs. “If he stays silent, he hands his rivals material to tell right-wing voters that the man who speaks of Zionism and security depends on a religious leadership that doubts Zionism itself.”

images.caption: Rabbi Dov Lando, spiritual leader of Israel's Degel HaTorah party [Creative Commons]

articles.title: 'Careless use of AI is the real threat - not the ghost stories'
articles.summary: Meredith Whittaker says the tech has been misunderstood, in an exclusive interview with BBC Global Women.
articles.body:
Warning: This article contains strong language.

Meredith Whittaker has little patience for the AI doom that dominates headlines - she thinks warnings of AI turning on humanity is a fear "not anchored in science".

"The risk is very real," says the boss of the Signal Foundation, which runs the encrypted messaging app of the same name, "but it's not the shiny ghost stories the wild-eyed boys are talking about".

Instead, she believes the more immediate danger is the technology being used carelessly.

She cites an alleged incident, reported by CNN, in which a chatbot used by US intelligence invented information about a Chinese vessel carrying nuclear material, reportedly leading the US to prepare a military response.

"We almost went to war with China," she tells BBC Global Women.

"A system that produces faulty intelligence and almost gets us into a war with China should not be considered super-intelligent by any standards."

Signal has an estimated 40-70 million users - a drop in the ocean next to WhatsApp, which has billions.

But it is renowned for its tough stance on protecting users' privacy - it hides who is sending a message from its own servers, limiting the data available to outside observers or hackers.

Time magazine named Whittaker one of the most powerful people in AI. She moves through the rooms where its future is discussed, from Silicon Valley boardrooms to Downing Street, Davos and the Vatican.

She studied literature at university and joined Google in 2006 as an entry-level temp with no computer science degree.

In late 2017, she made her name when a colleague told her about Project Maven, a secret Google contract with the US Department of Defense to build AI for drone targeting.

She understood what it meant to "compress the kill chain": to shrink the time between a machine flagging a target and someone deciding to fire, reducing deliberation. With thousands of colleagues, she pushed back.

"This is going to launder bad intelligence and bad data," she remembers arguing publicly.

The following year Whittaker helped organise a walkout, in which some 20,000 staff protested against the company's handling of several issues, including what they felt was the rushed introduction of new technology. Google dropped the contract and Palantir picked it up.

She draws a direct line from Maven to the US missile attack on a school in Iran this year, which she says relied on the system and on outdated intelligence that identified the school as a military target.

"This is exactly what we were warning about in 2017," she says.

In response, Palantir told Global Women there was "no evidence that Palantir's software was at fault in this terrible tragedy".

It added that "Palantir is not responsible for the underlying data nor identifying intelligence deficiencies". And earlier this year it's UK and Europe boss, Louis Mosley told the BBC that "there's always a human in the loop, so there is always a human that makes the ultimate decision".

The US military has yet to release the findings of its investigation into the Minab strike, but Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said it would "never target civilian targets".

Governments, including the UK's, argue for more access to conversations on messaging apps. They say this is to protect women and children.

At London Tech Week 2026, then Prime Minister Keir Starmer said technology companies would be expected to detect and block nude images on children's devices, or face legislation.

Whittaker argues children would be able to circumvent any such measures, calling the government's approach "an unprecedented regime of communication and information controls".

The Department for Science, Innovation and Technology told the BBC it is preparing legislation.

Would Signal leave any country, the UK included, that forced it to weaken its encryption?

"Yes! My God, I have a backbone," she says. "It doesn't change based on mood. It doesn't change based on consultants."

Faced with exposing people "who rely on us, sometimes in the context of life or death, to surveillance that could be weaponised against them", she says, "we would leave the market".

The app is fully or partially blocked in Russia, China and Iran.

Rani Govender, Head of Child Safety Online at the National Society for Prevention of Cruelty to Children, told the BBC it hears from children who have been groomed and moved on to end-to-end encrypted platforms, where they are coerced into creating child sexual abuse material.

"Tech companies are responsible for the design choices they make, and they cannot ignore the risks those choices can create for children."

But Signal does have support from some women's groups, often those from the Global South who use the app themselves.

"In a time of state surveillance and cyber-attacks, Signal is a tool for survival," says Hera Hussain, founder of the gender abuse charity Chayn, which is active throughout South Asia.

"With any platform, it can be used by bad actors too, and we have to hold that truth too."

I put to Whittaker a case from Canada, where police officers shared racist and misogynistic messages in a Signal group which leaked only when one of them passed it on to the media.

A lawyer for one officer said the men believed Signal was as private and safe as their own home.

"If they had that conversation in the kitchen and their bro snitched, would it be: 'What are we doing about kitchens?'" she asks.

"It has to work for everyone or it works for no-one. This is the principle of fundamental rights. They apply even to assholes."

She points to a US woman jailed after Meta handed over messages showing she helped her daughter access abortion in a state where it had been criminalised.

Private communication, she says, protects people from many kinds of harm - "an abusive spouse, a misogynist law enforcement officer with access to a database, or an authoritarian government that doesn't think women should get educated".

What would she want to say to a woman who wants to enter the tech field but is intimidated by the gendered aspect of the profession?

"Do you sit down at a terminal and feel a rush of energy? Do you enjoy playing with and defining AI systems?"

Then she pauses and says: "Are you able to navigate interesting and gnarly environments where not everyone is going to be chill? Because there's nothing more dangerous than being a coward in front of a bully."

I ask her if these environments are full of bullies.

Her colleague says, "I think that's 2pm" - the time we agreed to end the interview.

Meredith smiles. "I'd say don't be a simp," she says, using a term for someone who shows extreme deference to authority figures.

"It's not going to help you. Don't laugh at the joke if you don't think it's funny."

This is part of the Global Women series from the BBC World Service, sharing untold and important stories from around the globe

articles.title: ‘Lot of talk about one company’: Centre tells satcom firms to meet security norms amid Musk's Starlink row
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Communications minister Jyotiraditya Scindia on Friday said satellite communication (satcom) companies can begin operations in India only after
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Communications minister Jyotiraditya Scindia on Friday said satellite communication (satcom) companies can begin operations in India only after individually meeting the required security conditions and milestones, stressing that three companies have received licences despite the focus on Elon Musk’s Starlink. He also took a dig at Congress for their response to Musk's statements.“There is a lot of conversation about one specific company, but three companies have got satcom licences,” Scindia said, underlining that each operator must fulfil the required conditions before it can start services.Scindia’s remarks come amid a row between Musk and the Indian government over the delay in Starlink’s commercial launch in the country. The SpaceX chief had alleged that “certain oligarchs” were blocking the company to protect their “monopolistic chokehold” on the Indian market, without initially naming anyone.The government rejected the allegation, describing India’s regulatory framework for satellite communication services as “fair and non-discriminatory”. It said security assessments were underway for all three licensed operators and that each could move to the next stage of seeking spectrum assignment once the process was completed. The government called suggestions of discriminatory treatment “baseless and misconceived”.Minister of state for communications Chandra Sekhar Pemmasani said the security clearance issue was pending with the ministry of home affairs and had “nothing to do with one company”.Scindia also took a swipe at Congress saying that the party had earlier objected to a particular person getting a licence but was now aligned with the same person in questioning why the licence had not been granted. He accused the party of not knowing whether it was “going left or right”.The remarks come after Musk stepped up his criticism on Thursday, saying Starlink was licensed in more than 165 countries and had spent five years complying with Indian government requirements. He questioned why the company was still awaiting approval and asked whether industrialist Mukesh Ambani was the “real boss of India”.Leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi responded to Musk on X, writing: “Welcome to India, Elon. Wait till you discover the other guy.”Musk replied: “Thank you, Rahul. This is indeed troubling.”Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Hayden Panettiere’s ex Wladimir Klitschko gets legal status to protect their daughter’s inheritance
articles.summary: Actor Hayden Panettiere’s ex-fiancé, former boxer Wladimir Klitschko, was granted legal authority by a California court Thursday to protect Panettiere’s property for their 11-year-old daughter.
articles.body: LOS ANGELES — Actor Hayden Panettiere’s ex-fiancé, former boxer Wladimir Klitschko, was granted legal authority by a California court Thursday to protect Panettiere’s property for their 11-year-old daughter after the television star’s accidental overdose death left the girl as her sole heir. Klitschko had filed the urgent petition last week, saying that pieces of Panettiere’s property were being taken by federal law enforcement agents investigating her death and by an unnamed nonfamily member looking to sell them, with no one in a position to try to recover them for her daughter. Klitschko, a Ukrainian former world champion boxer, has had full custody of the girl, Kaya, for most of her life, and she has lived with him in Ukraine. The father and daughter appeared in Los Angeles County court remotely via videoconference. They spoke only to introduce themselves at the brief hearing with only Kaya visible on camera, sitting at a table in front of curtains. Judge Stephanie Santoro granted Klitschko the status of temporary guardian of Kaya’s estate until a long-term administrator can be appointed. Santoro asked Klitschko’s lawyer, Diane Park, why the matter was urgent. Park said they believed a person described only as a nonrelative had taken items after Panettiere’s death and had tried to sell some of her jewelry at a pawn shop. And she said assets were in danger of going unaccounted for during the death investigation. Court documents said authority was needed to deal with both the pawnshop owner and police agencies. Panettiere’s taxes also need to be filed this month, the lawyer said. Santoro, satisfied with the explanation, approved the move. Panettiere, the former star of the TV series “Heroes” and “Nashville,” was pronounced dead in an apartment in Greenville, South Carolina, on Aug. 16 at age 36 after paramedics found her unresponsive. A coroner’s report obtained by The Associated Press said her death was from an accidental overdose of several drugs, including fentanyl. She had been in rehab just weeks before. Her on-and-off boyfriend Brian Hickerson and his brother Zach Hickerson were at the home. Park told Santoro that the property, the pawnshop and the nonfamily member were in Los Angeles County, where the judge’s ruling held authority. Park declined to comment outside the courtroom. Klitschko’s Sept. 24 petition emphasized that his intention is solely to protect his daughter’s future assets until a permanent administrator can be put in place. “There is a high probability that property belonging to Hayden’s Estate may be lost, damaged or dissipated,” the document said. The filing said that before her death, Panettiere and Klitschko hired security to protect her home because an unnamed person had gained unauthorized access, and it’s expected the same person would continue to try to “misappropriate” her property. Panettiere’s mother, Lesley Vogel, filed a document saying she consented to Klitschko being appointed. Klitschko, 50, an Olympic gold medalist, held several heavyweight titles between 2000 and 2015. He and Panettiere began dating in 2009 and got engaged in 2013. His older brother Vitali, also a former champion boxer, is mayor of Kyiv, the Ukrainian capital. The two brothers, sons of a Soviet major general, have been prominent public figures in Ukraine during its war with Russia. In her memoir released earlier this year, Panettiere acknowledged being addicted to alcohol and having postpartum depression after her daughter’s birth in 2014. Kaya went to live with Klitschko full-time when she was 2. Panettiere’s father told investigators that when she died she had plans to visit her daughter in Ukraine days later.

images.caption: Wladimir Klitschko and Hayden Panettiere on Nov. 29, 2016 in Miami Beach, Fla.

articles.title: U.S. indictment charges Maduro with overseeing machine of repression, torture of Americans
articles.summary: U.S. prosecutors unveiled sweeping new criminal charges against former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro on Thursday, accusing him and his wife of heading a state-sponsored system of repression responsible for beating, asphyxiating, and delivering electric shocks to scores of victims, including several Americans.
articles.body: NEW YORK — U.S. prosecutors unveiled sweeping new criminal charges against former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro on Thursday, accusing him and his wife of heading a state-sponsored system of repression responsible for beating, asphyxiating, and delivering electric shocks to scores of victims, including several Americans. The torture charges add to pressure on the ousted authoritarian leader and his wife, Cilia Flores, who were seized from their Caracas home by the U.S. military in January to face drug trafficking charges in New York. The updated indictment “alleges conduct that is truly unthinkable,” U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said outside the Manhattan courthouse where the case is being handled. “This is the epitome of corruption.” Maduro denies the charges and “looks forward to his day in court,” lawyer Barry Pollack said. Flores’ attorney said he hadn’t yet had time to review the new allegations. The indictment claims Maduro suggested torture methods, sought and received updates on specific victims’ treatment, watched a video of a forced confession and personally threatened the killing of one prisoner’s child “as a form of psychological torture.” On occasion, he would laugh after hearing about the abuse of prisoners, prosecutors allege. Flores, a former attorney general, helped develop the repressive system and ordered the torture of some specific people, the indictment contends. Maduro, who served as Venezuela’s president from 2013 until his capture in January, has been under investigation for years by the International Criminal Court over allegations of crimes against humanity, tied to his crackdown on opponents. He has always denied any wrongdoing. He and his wife pleaded not guilty in the U.S. drug case, which accused them of conspiring to flood the U.S. with cocaine. Their attorneys have asked for the case to be dismissed on the grounds that they have immunity as the leader and first lady of a foreign country. Flores’ lawyers unsuccessfully asked a judge Thursday to release her on house arrest due to medical concerns. Alleged torture victims included U.S. citizens The revised indictment covers allegations of torture stretching back to Maduro’s ascent to power in 2013, when he took over as president from his mentor Hugo Chávez, who died of cancer that year. At the time, Maduro, a former bus driver lacking his predecessor’s military pedigree, was struggling to make inroads with the armed forces — historically the arbiter of political disputes in Venezuela — as the oil-dependent economy began spiraling out of control and government opponents took to the streets. Fearing a barracks revolt, Maduro authorized Venezuela’s feared DGCIM military intelligence agency to use torture against military insiders and opponents he saw as threatening his grip on power, prosecutors allege. While the indictment doesn’t name the alleged victims, the descriptions of the deaths and imprisonment match those of several high-profile Maduro opponents. They include Leopoldo López, who spent more than three years in prison for leading anti-government protests, and former Chávez Defense Minister Raúl Baduel, who died in custody in 2021. Also described is the shocking death of Fernando Albán, an opposition politician whose fall from the 10th floor of an intelligence agency building was later determined by a U.S. court to be a “murder for hire.” Three American victims of torture were also described in the indictment. One, who matches the description of Osman Khan, was detained entering Venezuela in early 2022 and was subjected to electric shocks and forced to eat his own vomit during eight months of imprisonment, the indictment says. Another was beaten badly enough to necessitate a long hospital stay and had a gun stuck in his mouth. A third was handcuffed, hooded and beaten for two days every half an hour, suffering a permanent eye injury, the indictment said. Khan was released in October 2022 along with former U.S. Marine corporal Matthew Heath and six American oil executives in exchange for two nephews of Flores jailed in the U.S. on narcotics convictions. He and Heath later sued in U.S. courts under a federal anti-terrorism law and, in May, won a $300 million default judgment against Maduro and other top Venezuelan officials for overseeing a pattern of torture. “It’s incredible to see a dictator in court,” Heath said Thursday upon learning of the new charges. “The Maduro prosecution will do more to prevent the kidnapping of Americans by rogue regimes than a hundred press releases from the United Nations.” Ex-Venezuelan spy chief is a key cooperator Torture is considered a grave crime under international law and can be prosecuted by any competent court, regardless of the victims’ nationality, said Kenneth Roth, a senior fellow at Yale University who for decades headed Human Rights Watch. Still, prosecution of foreign officials in the U.S. is exceedingly rare, having been attempted only a handful of times, including against the son of Liberian President Charles Taylor, Russians responsible for war crimes in Ukraine and a former prison warden in Bashar Assad’s Syria. “The problem here isn’t a lack of jurisdiction but rather selectivity of prosecution,” said Roth. Venezuela’s government has so far been silent about the new accusations against Maduro, reflecting the challenges facing acting President Delcy Rodríguez as she strives to appease the security forces without alienating President Donald Trump, whose support she can’t lose. Rodríguez, as Maduro’s vice president, for years oversaw key elements of Venezuela’s security apparatus, including a domestic spy agency accused of arbitrary detentions and other human rights abuses. One of Maduro’s co-defendants, Gen. Hugo Carvajal, pleaded guilty last year to the drug trafficking charges in New York after being extradited from Spain. Since then, Carvajal, who served as Chávez’s spymaster and head of the DGCIM for more than a decade, has been meeting with prosecutors building the case against Maduro. In an open letter to Trump last year, Carvajal, who broke with Maduro years ago, said he wanted “to atone by telling the full truth so that the United States can protect itself from the dangers I witnessed for so many years.” Former first lady denied release for medical treatment The new charges were unveiled as Flores, 69, was in court Thursday for a previously scheduled hearing over her request to be released so she can undergo medical treatment. Her lawyers have said she’s lost 25 pounds (11 kilograms) while imprisoned in the U.S., might have suffered a minor heart attack in July and has been told that she might need heart surgery. U.S. District Court Judge Alvin Hellerstein denied Flores’ request, siding with prosecutors who said she is an “extreme” flight risk. He also pushed back at the notion that her high blood pressure was life-threatening, noting she’s already on medication for that. Outside the courthouse, over a dozen demonstrators chanted slogans and held signs supporting her request.

articles.title: Why has Iraq decided to ban online map service Waze?
articles.summary: Iraq plans to ban Waze, citing Israeli origins, and suggests alternatives like Google Maps or local app in development.
articles.body:
Iraq is set to ban the popular navigation app Waze, which was founded in Israel.

Communications Minister Mustafa Sanad announced the move on Tuesday. It has prompted discussions in Iraq over whether the country can build its own alternative and whether banning one app protects users’ location data.

The Ministry of Communications plans to block the use of Waze by the end of December, according to the Iraqi newspaper Al-Mada.

Sanad told the broadcaster Rudaw that it would take effect some time at the start of 2027.

He made the announcement on the sidelines of the Hitex 2026 technology exhibition in Erbil, the capital of the semiautonomous Kurdish region in northern Iraq.

“Because it comes from the entity [Israel] and is Israeli-made, we will ban it at the beginning of 2027,” he said.

Waze is a widely used navigation app. Hundreds of motorists, including taxi drivers, use it to get around. The service relies on users to report traffic jams, accidents and police checkpoints as they happen.

It was developed in Israel, and Google bought it in 2013 for nearly $1bn.

Waze’s privacy policy lets it collect users’ locations, routes, destinations, search histories and device details, depending on their settings.

Pooled across many users over time, such data have security value because they can reveal movement patterns, peak times and unusual changes.

Rudaw reported that the app has been the subject of security discussions in Iraq over its alerts being used to avoid checkpoints although Sanad did not link the ban to that issue.

Why does the Israeli connection matter in Iraq?

Iraq does not recognise Israel or have diplomatic relations with it and has formally been at war with it since 1948.

A 2022 law criminalises any diplomatic, political, military, economic or cultural ties with Israel. Its penalties include life imprisonment and the death penalty. It was passed by 275 votes in the 329-seat Council of Representatives.

The law applies to all Iraqi citizens, state institutions and media as well as private companies and foreign entities operating in the country, including the Kurdish region.

Sanad has not specifically said Waze must be blocked under the antinormalisation law.

Distrust of Israel has been bolstered by the US-Israel war on Iran. The United States and its allies have targeted Iraq’s Iran-aligned militias with air strikes and economic measures.

During the war, Iraq also faced a serious case of Israeli infiltration. In May, US media reported that Israel had built two secret military outposts deep inside Iraq’s desert to support its war on Iran.

One post was nearly exposed by a local shepherd who stumbled upon it and was killed.

What alternatives is the government offering?

Sanad said users could switch to Google Maps or Iraqi navigation apps.

Communications Ministry spokesman Omar al-Amiri said in remarks carried by Al-Mada that Waze would be replaced by a yet-to-be-named Iraqi app.

He said the app would run without technical problems.

Al-Mada also quoted Iraqi technology researcher Mustafa Kamel al-Sharif as saying a national alternative would take more than an app with an Iraqi map and logo.

It would need accurate geographic databases, a constantly updated road network, routing systems and live data on traffic, accidents and closures, he said.

He also told the newspaper that the crux of the issue lies in how Iraq regulates its citizens’ data and other services may also collect sensitive data similar to Waze.

The ministry has not said how the block will be enforced or whether it will cover the Kurdish region. It has also not set out the ban’s legal basis or said when the Iraqi app will launch.

Another unknown is why Google Maps, owned by the same parent company, Alphabet, would remain available or serve as an alternative.

The government has also not answered why Waze is being banned now when its Israeli roots have been long known.
