articles.title: Christa Pike makes ‘remarkable’ recovery from 'death' after failed US botched execution
articles.summary: Christa Pike, the Tennessee death row inmate who survived a botched lethal injection attempt last week, has made a “profound” recovery and can now walk
articles.body: Christa Pike, the Tennessee death row inmate who survived a botched lethal injection attempt last week, has made a “profound” recovery and can now walk with assistance and eat, her lawyers said on Thursday.Pike, 50, was left in critical condition after two injections of the execution drug pentobarbital failed to kill her on September 30. Her lawyers said she had also regained some movement in her arms, which were badly injured during the attempted execution.“Physicians are encouraged by her physical recovery,” her legal team said in a statement, describing her progress as “remarkable”, BBC reported.However, Pike continues to struggle with the psychological trauma of surviving the failed execution, her lawyers said.“Christa is dealing with the profound psychological trauma of having survived a failed execution, including the terror, pain and uncertainty of believing she was about to die,” they said.Emotional and psychological impact unclearHer legal team added that the full emotional and psychological impact of the incident remained unclear and that it was uncertain how long her recovery would take. Despite the ordeal, Pike continued to express concern for others, particularly the family of her victim, Colleen Slemmer, they said.Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of Slemmer, a 19-year-old schoolmate whom she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed after meeting her at a job training camp for low-income young people.Pike was 18 at the time of the killing, while Shipp was 17. He was spared the death penalty because he was not legally an adult when the crime was committed and remains in prison.Slemmer’s mother, who had supported Pike’s execution, described the failed attempt as a “mess”.Court orders preservation of evidenceThe failed execution has raised questions about what went wrong and whether Tennessee could attempt to execute Pike again.On Wednesday, Judge I’Ashea Myles ordered officials to preserve all evidence related to the botched procedure, potentially laying the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state.Meanwhile, some proponents of capital punishment have suggested using a different execution method.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘Arrest me, detain me’: CJP's Abhijeet Dipke defies Delhi Police ban, says October 10 Jantar Mantar protest will go ahead
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) activist Abhijeet Dipke on Friday said the organisation would go ahead with its October 10 protest at Delhi’s
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) activist Abhijeet Dipke on Friday said the organisation would go ahead with its October 10 protest at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar despite Delhi Police denying permission, adding that its members were prepared to face arrest.Slamming the restrictions imposed ahead of the demonstration, Dipke questioned the decision to curtail public transport and said the measures would cause inconvenience to ordinary commuters.“What is this fear? Why are you this scared? You are scared of the youth in the country. You shut down trains, you shut down metro, what should one do?” he said.Dipke also questioned the government’s justification for the restrictions, arguing that shutting down metro services, cancelling trains and blocking roads would create the very inconvenience authorities cited as a concern.“Is Delhi a property of Narendra Modi or Amit Shah? Is this their ancestral property? Is this their paternal property? On one hand, you say that due to the protest, people are facing inconvenience, and on the other hand, you shut down all the metro, you shut down all the railways, you block all the roads. Now, won't there be inconvenience for people?” he said.Asserting that the activists would not back down, Dipke challenged the authorities to detain or arrest them.“How many people will they detain? Arrest me, detain me! Saurabh is ready, Ashutosh is ready. Arrest me, detain me!” he said.Dipke questioned the need for police permission to hold a demonstration at Jantar Mantar, which is a designated protest site. Referring to Article 19 of the Constitution, he argued that the proposed demonstration was an exercise of the activists’ constitutional rights.He also raised questions about Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and alleged changes relating to Form 6, asking why permission should be required to protest against the poll authority.“Did Gyanesh Kumar take permission? Before deleting 13 crore votes, did Gyanesh Kumar take permission? The Supreme Court didn't even give approval for the Form 6 modification. So, when Gyanesh Kumar, without telling anyone, without asking anyone, deletes 13 crore votes, then to protest against him, the constitutional right we have according to Article 19, what is the need for permission?” he said.Dipke further criticised the government over the restrictions, saying Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union home minister Amit Shah should be concerned about the opposition being voiced by young people.“The government is very serious. I think Narendra Modi and Amit Shah should keep checking their blood pressure. The kind of fear this government is showing,” he said.Why Delhi Police denied permissionDelhi Police has denied permission for the October 10 protest, citing the short notice, alleged non-compliance with directions during an earlier demonstration and concerns over public safety, law and order and traffic management.Joint commissioner of police Nupur Prasad said the New Delhi district received an application on October 7 from Saurabh Das, CJP co-convener, informing the police about the proposed demonstration seeking accountability from the Chief Election Commissioner.Prasad said the notice was submitted too close to the planned date, as the prescribed guidelines require applications to be received at least 10 days before a protest.She also alleged that CJP members had failed to comply with lawful directions and undertakings given during an earlier protest for which permission had been granted.“In the New Delhi area, Section 163 of the BNSS (Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita) is in operation, under which, to maintain public order and safety, a reasonable preventive restriction is in place,” Prasad said.She warned that legal action would be taken against anyone violating the provisions of Section 163 of the BNSS.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: Cars torched and shops looted as anti-migrant violence erupts in South Africa
articles.summary: South Africa has experienced recurrent outbreaks of violence, often targeting migrants from neighbouring countries.
articles.body:
At least 24 vehicles have been set ablaze and foreign-owned shops looted in South Africa as anti-immigration protests descended into violence in two major cities, police say.

Unrest broke out on Thursday in Soweto, a sprawling township outside Johannesburg, the country's largest city, and Durban, a major port on the east coast.

The violence comes amid growing anger over a court ruling which would allow some migrants who had arrived in the country illegally to apply for asylum.

This had led to long queues outside immigration centres and the government on Friday said it would change the way it would comply with that ruling, without giving details.

The Department of Home Affairs said the current policy had seen its staff "overwhelmed", while "serious threats to public safety and order had emerged".

It said that the new policy would still abide by the Constitutional Court ruling.

South Africa has experienced repeated outbreaks of xenophobic violence, often targeting migrants from neighbouring countries.

Thursday's demonstration turned violent following allegations that a foreign national had assaulted one of the protesters in Durban.

Three foreign nationals were arrested in connection with the alleged assault, police said.

In Durban, in the eastern province of KwaZulu-Natal, protesters gathered outside a government refugee reception centre demanding that it stop accepting asylum applications.

Police fired rubber bullets to disperse crowds as businesses in the city centre shut their doors.

"There were clashes between foreign nationals in the area and South African nationals," senior local police officer Xolani Fihla told state broadcaster SABC.

"At the present moment, I can confirm that no injuries have been reported," he added.

Police said 14 vehicles were torched in Durban and 10 in Soweto, where gunshots were also reported during confrontations between residents and foreign shopkeepers.

Acting national police commissioner Lt Gen Puleng Dimpane condemned the destruction of property.

In Orlando West, a neighbourhood of Soweto, residents had initially gathered to demand the closure of small convenience stores, known locally as spaza shops, operated by foreign nationals.

Protesters forced foreign traders out of some areas, while shops were attacked and a building was set on fire, local media reported.

Police said reinforcements had been deployed to prevent further violence.

The authorities have promised to pursue those responsible for the destruction.

The latest unrest follows a July ruling by Constitutional Court, South Africa's highest court, which struck down restrictions preventing some people from seeking asylum because of how they entered the country or missed immigration deadlines.

The judgment means asylum seekers must be allowed to submit applications, even if they entered South Africa without the required documents.

This prompted hundreds of people to gather at refugee reception centres, fuelling anger among anti-immigration campaigners who fear the decision will encourage undocumented migration.

Government spokesman William Baloyi told Reuters news agency that people had deliberately spread false claims about the judgment, creating the impression that undocumented migrants would automatically be granted legal status.

Baloyi insisted that the ruling does not automatically give migrants refugee status or the right to remain permanently in South Africa.

Officials say applications will still be assessed individually and applicants will remain subject to immigration checks.

The protests forced tens of thousands of migrants to flee, with some returning home through repatriation programmes organised by their governments.

South Africa has struggled with xenophobic attacks for nearly two decades. In 2008, more than 60 people were killed and tens of thousands displaced during widespread attacks on foreign nationals.

The latest unrest comes against a backdrop of widespread poverty, deep inequality and unemployment affecting roughly a third of the workforce.

Migrants are frequently accused of taking jobs, contributing to crime and placing pressure on public services, although researchers say such sweeping claims are not supported by evidence.

Despite its economic difficulties, South Africa remains one of the continent's main destinations for migrants seeking employment, safety and better opportunities.

Additional reporting by Christian Parkinson in Johannesburg

articles.title: Renault Duster Hybrid fuel-efficiency revealed: Beats Grand Vitara, Hyryder
articles.summary: Renault has opened bookings for the Duster Hybrid ahead of its October 17 launch in India.
articles.body: Renault has opened bookings for the Duster Hybrid ahead of its October 17 launch in India. The SUV has an ARAI-certified fuel efficiency rating of 29 km/l, exceeding the claimed figures of the Maruti Suzuki Grand Vitara and Toyota Urban Cruiser Hyryder strong hybrids by 1.03 km/l.Called the Hybrid E-Tech 160, the new variant uses a 1.8-litre naturally aspirated four-cylinder petrol engine paired with two electric motors. The setup comprises a 20 BHP generator and a 48 BHP motor, producing a combined 168 BHP and 172 Nm of torque. Power is delivered to the front wheels.The hybrid system uses a 1.4 kWh battery and an eight-speed dedicated hybrid transmission (DHT) with fixed gear ratios. It manages the petrol engine and electric motors based on driving conditions, allowing electric-only operation when suitable and recovering energy during braking and deceleration.The Duster Hybrid will join the existing 1.0-litre Turbo TCe 100 petrol engine, which produces 99 BHP and 166 Nm, and the 1.3-litre Turbo TCe 160 unit, generating 161 BHP and 280 Nm.The new variant will become the fourth strong-hybrid option in the mid-size SUV segment, alongside the Toyota Urban Cruiser Hyryder and Maruti Suzuki Grand Vitara and Victoris. Bookings are available through Renault India’s website and authorised dealerships. The Maruti Suzuki Victoris comes closest to the Duster Hybrid’s claimed fuel efficiency, with a difference of 0.35 km/l.

articles.title: Japan’s Okinawa calls for review of US forces pact after killing
articles.summary: Assembly on the island, where tens of thousands of US soldiers are stationed, seeks change after Marine arrested.
articles.body:
The prefectural assembly of Okinawa has called for a review of an agreement overseeing the stationing of United States military forces on the Japanese island.

The assembly adopted the resolution on Friday. The vote came after a US Marine was accused of robbing and killing a local woman.

The call to adapt the Japan-US Status of Forces Agreement to urge the US military to prevent such incidents will be sent to the US embassy. The assembly also passed a statement to the same effect addressed to the Japanese government.

Ryotaro Odo, who heads the assembly’s special committee on US military bases, said the US military was “not functioning as an organisation”, pointing to failures in training and discipline.

He called the killing “extremely heinous and despicable” and urged the military to cooperate with investigators and discipline those responsible.

Some of the assembly’s members opposed the resolution because it failed to demand the dismissal of the US military chief in Okinawa, Japan’s Kyodo News agency reported.

Lance-Corporal Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, has been accused of killing Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in Naha on Saturday. He has denied the allegations.

The case has sparked a series of demonstrations in Tokyo and Okinawa.

The island hosts the majority of the 54,000 US soldiers stationed in Japan. Crimes including rapes, assaults, hit-and-run and drink-driving incidents by US personnel have long sparked protests.

The US military paused its operations for 48 hours from Wednesday and also imposed a 30-day curfew from midnight to 5am starting on Friday.

Tokyo has called in the US ambassador and the US forces commander in Okinawa to protest the incident, and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has condemned the “heinous” crime.

Okinawa, which was under US control from 1945 to 1972, still hosts many facilities used exclusively by US forces.

The island’s assembly passed a similar resolution in 2024 after a series of sexual assaults by US servicemen came to light with the municipal assemblies of Naha, Ginowan, Miyakojima and Motobu filing protests.

articles.title: In new Elon Musk documentary, his lieutenants are the most damning voices
articles.summary: ‘Musk,’ the new film from Alex Gibney, features interviews with more than the usual critics of the Tesla and SpaceX CEO.
articles.body: SAN RAFAEL, Calif. — It’s easy to find people with bad things to say about tech magnate Elon Musk, and plenty of those people show up in “Musk,” a new documentary about his rise to political and corporate power. What’s more surprising in the film are the unflattering statements by some of his own employees, including ones who still work for him. Some of the harshest scenes in the film, which opens Friday in Los Angeles and New York, are ones in which Musk’s lieutenants were recorded on video or in audio as they wielded power on his behalf or discussed what they had already done for him. Warning: This article includes spoilers for the documentary “Musk.” There are clips of Ashok Elluswamy, a high-ranking Tesla engineer, acknowledging in a videotaped deposition that an infamous hype video he helped put together in 2016 about the company’s self-driving capabilities was not an accurate representation of Tesla’s technology at the time. There are also audio snippets from Jared Birchall, who handles Musk’s personal matters. He is heard on a recording of a phone call with online influencer Ashley St. Clair, shortly after she had given birth to a child she and Musk conceived, in which he plays hardball on child support arrangements. Both incidents were documented in the media: Reuters reported in 2023 on the transcript of Elluswamy’s deposition, and The Wall Street Journal reported last year on Birchall’s phone call with St. Clair. But the video and the audio appear to be newly public, giving the documentary a mix of voices beyond the usual critics and creating moments of surprise even for a viewer who is familiar with the ins and outs of Musk’s complicated story. Filmmaker Alex Gibney says in the documentary that he and his team spent more than three years researching Musk, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, pulling together not only archival interviews and hard-to-find footage but also a database of quotes from Musk that are peppered throughout the film. Musk, 55, did not participate in the documentary, and he has panned it, saying on X that it is a “hit piece” and that Gibney has “zero integrity.” Musk, Tesla, SpaceX, Elluswamy and Birchall did not respond to requests for comment. The nearly four-hour film is a comprehensive tour through Musk’s life story, with deep dives into the growth of SpaceX and Tesla, his fathering of 14 known children and his on-again, off-again alliance with President Donald Trump, including his becoming the biggest donor to Trump’s 2024 campaign. The film is a reminder of how often Musk has put himself at the center of public discourse and pop culture, and it moves swiftly through the highlights and lowlights: from his 2021 hosting gig on “Saturday Night Live” and his chaotic purchase of Twitter the next year to his Grok chatbot’s embracing the identity “MechaHitler” and his wielding of a chain saw early in Trump’s second term. “I like to call it a ‘svelte’ four-hour film,” producer Jessie Deeter said at a screening Wednesday at the Mill Valley Film Festival in Marin County, California. (The film has a 10-minute intermission, but it is still roughly the length of the 1962 epic “Lawrence of Arabia.”) At the screening, which was about 90% full, the biggest applause came during a moment of anti-Musk defiance, as a former career federal employee explained why they quit the Trump administration last year rather than cooperate with Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency. The film lands at another potentially pivotal moment for Musk, amid speculation that Democrats may investigate him if they take control of Congress after the midterm elections. Polling shows that Musk remains deeply divisive, with a majority of Americans holding unfavorable views of him even as Trump honored him at the White House on Thursday. The documentary demonstrates that Musk’s dabbling in politics is nothing new: Archival videos show that, years before he endorsed Trump in 2024, Musk was rubbing elbows with politicians such as former California Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, and the late Sen. Dianne Feinstein, D-Calif., and getting benefits in return, such as low-emission credits for Tesla. Part of what drives the documentary forward is how it crosses genres: Parts of it feel like a political thriller or a legal whodunit, while others are like a video game simulation, a science fiction fantasy or a celebrity tabloid drama. Other moments are closer to a horror film, especially as Gibney narrates some of the graphic details of collisions involving Tesla’s driver-assistance software. He includes, for example, dashcam video from a 2019 crash in which a Tesla on “Autopilot” ran a stop sign in Florida and killed a pedestrian — a crash for which a jury found Tesla 33% at fault and ordered it to pay $243 million in damages. One of the people interviewed in the film, science fiction author and tech activist Cory Doctorow, adds to the grim feeling by wearing a guillotine pin on his lapel. Later, the documentary lingers again on death, as Gibney tries to tally the human cost of Musk’s drive last year to dismantle the U.S. Agency for International Development. Between shots of malnourished children in Africa and elsewhere, Samantha Power, who was a USAID administrator during the Biden administration, says the cuts froze some food programs for the world’s poor and blames the cuts for 14 million potential deaths. (The number is based on a projection published last year estimating possible deaths over the following five years.) In the film’s rendering, the horror of those statistics and images stands in stark contrast with Musk’s ongoing obsession: traveling deeper into space, including to Mars, for the potential benefit of future, unborn generations. A few parts of the film are presented without evidence or explanation. Gibney boosts a conspiracy theory that Musk used his Starlink constellation of internet satellites to meddle in the 2024 election — an unfounded idea that independent fact-checkers have long criticized. He also raises concerns about potential data collection by Starlink satellites and by Tesla vehicles but does not go beyond vague theories. A more pressing question the film wrestles with is whether or how much Musk has changed over his years in the public spotlight. The film repeatedly shows a younger Musk who is not only physically different, with thinner hair and a slighter build, but also speaking about different issues from those he addresses now — including “oil addiction,” an old motivation behind growing Tesla. Another of Musk’s associates, former SpaceX engineer Jim Cantrell, says in the film that Musk has changed less than some people may imagine. “Success has allowed him to take the lid off what he’s really thinking,” he says.

articles.title: Hunger grips a rural community hit by Trump’s cuts
articles.summary: Those on the front lines of feeding their neighbors in rural West Virginia say they face unprecedented challenges brought on by Washington.
articles.body: DUNLOW, W.Va. — Bill Likens stared down a half-mile-long line of cars that started forming before the sun came up over the Appalachian Mountains. He had one job: figure out how to feed them all. Some had driven more than 30 miles in aging cars and trucks that wheezed down flood-prone roads through the steep hills. They sat silently as the temperature rose into the 80s, their vehicles turned off with no air conditioning to preserve gas, waiting hours for a few boxes of food. Aided by a cane, Likens, 51, surveyed the pallets being unloaded off a semitruck that arrived that morning. He counted cartons of eggs and sacks of potatoes to calculate how much each waiting car could get — an algorithm of hunger he is constantly trying to solve. “There’s a decent chance we could run out,” said Likens, who runs the food pantry in Dunlow as director of community outreach for Cabwaylingo Presbyterian Chapel, a small brick church he attended growing up. “I don’t want them to sit in that line and not get anything,” he said. “But I don’t have a lot of extra food these days.” Increasingly, the job of feeding the nation’s hungry is falling on the shoulders of everyday Americans like Likens, who have become the last bulwark against hunger in a land of plenty. Likens and others on the front lines of feeding their neighbors say they face unprecedented challenges brought on by Washington. Food distribution programs are getting less food from federal programs to feed the hungry after cuts by the Trump administration. At the same time, restrictions on food stamps from the Republicans’ “big, beautiful bill” have driven up demand, while rising gas prices because of the Iran war have cut into the budgets of households and food banks alike. The challenges extend far beyond Appalachia. An NBC News survey of 48 of the largest food banks across 35 states and Washington, D.C., found that nearly three-quarters said more people are showing up at their doors over the past year, from workers on their lunch breaks to older adults overwhelmed with medical expenses. At the same time, more than 80% said the food and funding they received through the U.S. Department of Agriculture had dropped and they were struggling with higher fuel costs for transporting food. In Maine, Good Shepherd Food Bank said the USDA cut the amount of food it received from 13 million pounds to 9 million pounds in one year. A Michigan food bank, Forgotten Harvest, said it’s handing out less food to make sure there is enough to go around: one bag of potatoes instead of two, two tubs of yogurt as opposed to six. “People are facing multiple hits to their budgets,” said Poonam Gupta, a senior research associate at the Urban Institute, a think tank that researches social and economic issues. “It is really difficult to find a way to continue affording a healthy and nutritious and balanced diet when you just have these constant hits.” Food banks’ struggles started in the early days of President Donald Trump’s second term when officials cut a $400 million Covid-era program to supply food banks with food from local farmers and paused an estimated $500 million in other planned food purchases by the USDA. Funding from Congress for a separate decades-old program to supply food banks with emergency food assistance has increased over the past several years, but many food bank leaders said they’re still getting less overall than during the Biden administration. Trump also signed into law the new restrictions on who can receive Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits, or food stamps, requiring nearly all able-bodied adults not caring for young children to work, volunteer or go to school at least 80 hours a month. Since the law was enacted, more than 5 million people, including at least 1 million children, have lost their food benefits. White House spokesperson Anna Kelly defended the administration’s policies, saying Trump is “uplifting every American’s financial situation” through tax cuts and efforts to increase jobs and business investments. “President Trump is strengthening SNAP for the Americans who need it by ensuring these programs are sustainable for future generations,” Kelly said, including measures to “crack down on waste, fraud and abuse.” The USDA said it hasn’t reduced the amount of food it provides. “Every day, the Food and Nutrition Administration invests $340 million in low-income communities and people in need of nutrition assistance, including millions of school children, elderly, and the disabled,” a USDA spokesperson said. “The mission to help those in need has not changed.” While those on the ground say they are thankful for everything they get, they are struggling to do more with less. Facing Hunger Foodbank, which supplies Likens’ pantry and others across Appalachia, has seen a 25% increase in the number of people seeking help over the past year, while the amount of food the federal government supplies has fallen by a third, CEO Cyndi Kirkhart said. Those forces have hit especially hard in areas that were already struggling economically, like West Virginia’s once-flourishing coal mining communities. The spike in gas costs means a 45-minute drive to the nearest grocery store can set residents back more than $15. And West Virginians who must comply with the new work requirements to receive food benefits are confronting a lack of jobs and training programs. Since last summer, about 24,000 people, including 8,000 children, have lost food stamps, according to the West Virginia Department of Human Services. “It’s like the pandemic on steroids without funds,” Kirkhart said. “I don’t believe the government needs to provide everything, but if you’re going to ask us to, please help.” Keeping neighbors fed Likens learned the tricks of how to battle an aching emptiness in his stomach early in life. When he was 12, his father, a construction supervisor for a coal mine, was injured by a falling piece of equipment. Suddenly, his family of seven had to live off of just $350 a month in government assistance. Growing up, there were days he ate only two meals, and he was never full. His mother often made biscuits and gravy because it was relatively filling. For the first week of the month, she had enough powdered milk to make the gravy. For the rest of the month, she mixed water, oil and a bit of flour. It had the appearance of gravy but not the flavor. The family survived with help from the same church he works for today. He and his wife, Addie, whom he met playing in the middle school band, live in the church house he and his brothers helped build as teenagers to repay the church for the food it had provided. In this corner of West Virginia, hunger is nothing new. For decades, the coal mining jobs that built many of the communities here have been leaving; the last mine near Dunlow closed more than a decade ago. Attracting new industries has been a struggle with little flat land, limited internet service and aging infrastructure. As the jobs left, so did many of the area’s younger residents, leaving a large population of seniors, including many raising grandchildren, who rely on Social Security as their only income. Likens said making sure no one goes hungry in his hometown has never been harder. His pantry, which serves 700 to 800 households, has gotten 25% less food from the USDA over the past several years, he said. The amount varies month to month, making it difficult to plan. In August, he got just 2.5 pounds of food per household, compared with the 20 pounds he was getting monthly several years ago. Meat has become a rarity, replaced by items like dried beans, which can be difficult to cook with for those with disabilities or children preparing their own meals. “This is the leanest we’ve been in the 23 years I’ve been doing this,” Likens said. The USDA said it hasn’t changed the type of food it sends. “States are responsible for ordering — based on supply and demand — and while no significant changes have been seen, the Trump administration has indeed prioritized increased purchases of fruits, vegetables, seafood and other proteins,” the spokesperson said. Likens said he has become increasingly dependent on food donations from private companies and food purchased by Facing Hunger, the West Virginia food bank that supplies his pantry and others. Everything he can get helps, but it’s not always the most nutritious food: His pantry was recently lined with 5-foot-high pallets of donated Peeps and more than 100,000 packages of Mike and Ike candy from other nonprofits. Canned pork has become a food pantry delicacy. “We need to recognize the fact that it does hurt people when we cut these programs that are so necessary,” Likens said. Along with running the food pantry, Likens started a backpack meals program in which every child at the nearby schools gets a small shopping bag of food to take home on the weekends. Volunteers pack the 250 bags each week with things kids can easily fix for themselves — a box of mac and cheese, a cereal bar, a Cup Noodles. “When I was a kid, this would have been my dream to have at home,” he said. “To be able to get a Chef Boyardee and a little juice.” Disappointed in Washington With the food for that day unloaded, Likens looked on as cars and trucks started slowly rolling through and an assembly line of volunteers began placing boxes in trunks and truck beds. Among the offerings: a carton of eggs, half a gallon of milk, a 5-pound bag of potatoes, around five pieces of cooked chicken, a pack of Jimmy Dean turkey sausage and a bag of apples. Facing Hunger purchased nearly all of the food that day with the money it gets from private donations, state funding and grants. The only items that came from the USDA were packs of sliced Swiss cheese. Inside a small SUV was Joanne Girvin, who waited her turn with her one-eyed Yorkshire terrier, Jasper, sitting on her lap. Girvin, 73, used to own a restaurant nearby and is now living off Social Security, which is barely enough to cover her monthly bills. Already on a tight budget, she has no extra room for $4 gallons of gas or a rising electric bill. That has left one place to cut — her food. She said she has lost 20 pounds over the past year because she has been eating less. The night before, she’d eaten canned deer meat left over from last fall’s hunting season with rice and gravy. Some nights she eats a bag of frozen broccoli with butter. “Sometimes I just sit down and cry when I’m trying to figure out what you’re going to eat out of a can or something because you don’t have no meat,” Girvin said as her eyes welled with tears. “It’s just really bad, this economy. It’s horrible.” Girvin has chickens in her backyard that she relies on for eggs, and this hunting season she and her husband plan to get more deer meat to feed themselves through the winter. When food is running low for her dog, she goes out and hunts a squirrel for him. For a bit of extra money, she sells some of her old belongings at flea markets. She said she doesn’t think those in Washington understand the struggle she and her neighbors face. “We need help,” she said. “They just don’t know the half of it. They really don’t.” It was a frustration echoed by others who showed up that morning in a state that Trump won in 2024 with 70% of the vote. While some supported Trump’s decision to attack Iran despite the higher gas prices and argued Republicans were an improvement over Democrats, others said Trump should be doing more to lower prices. A few cars behind Girvin in line was Bonnie Newsome. She used to drive a school bus, but now, like Girvin, she’s struggling to afford groceries on her retirement income. Asked whether she had a message for Trump, she said: “I love you, but I think you can do a better job than what you’re doing.” Over the past year, she has been hit by a string of higher costs, including her electric bill, groceries and gas. With winter coming, she’s worried about affording propane to heat her house. “I really thought President Trump would move right on in and take care of everything,” Newsome said. “He’s disappointed me, he has.” Without help from Washington, she relies on people like Likens. She has known him since he was a child and she was driving the school bus. “If it weren’t for this food pantry that Bill’s doing, we would be in trouble. We really would,” Newsome said. “I used to pick Bill up when he was a kid and drive him to school, and now he’s taking care of me.” ‘We stick together here’ About an hour away from Likens’ pantry, Donna Paterino was doing her own calculus of how to feed more mouths with less food. Her pantry, tucked in the back room of a firehouse, serves more than 200 households a month, twice as many as a year ago, while the quantity and quality of the food she’s getting from the USDA has declined, she said. The USDA deliveries are often less filling and difficult for seniors to cook with, like a recent influx of chickpeas. “I live by faith and not by sight. But if I’m looking, I see a bunch of people in Washington who are out of touch,” Paterino said. Before she started Widow’s Mite Food Pantry 15 years ago in Matewan, a town made famous for a 1920s shootout between supporters of coal miners and representatives of the mine owners, Paterino, 60, worked for years at school cafeterias, where she saw the signs of hunger in her community. Students, many being raised by grandparents, would quietly ask her for an extra portion at lunch; one told her all there was to eat at home was a bottle of ranch dressing; another was so thin her pants were held up by a rope. Now, she said, the faces of those she’s serving have changed. “My focus used to be just the seniors and grandparents raising grandchildren,” she said. “Now, I have just as many middle-class families who reach out and say: ‘Do you have anything left that I can use? Do you have any juice I can give the kids until Monday?’” To fill the gaps, Paterino is left scrambling for donations. Each week, she picks up cast-off food from a nearby Dollar General, which gives her items like milk a few days before its sell-by date or dozens of damaged boxes of cereal. She recently got a call from the Dollar General store manager when one of its freezers went out, telling her to get there as soon as she could to collect the food, which included frozen burritos and Hot Pockets, before it defrosted. Within 20 minutes, in the pouring rain, she was there with a volunteer to load it up, and days later those items had helped 12 families get through the end of the month until their food stamp benefits rolled over. Once her food leaves the pantry, she often sees it continue to trickle throughout the community — a senior will give their milk to a family with young kids, and a family will make a pot of soup for a neighbor. In Mingo County, where Paterino runs her small pantry, 1 in 3 children live in poverty, and the population has declined by 9% since 2020. One in 7 working-age adults receive Social Security disability benefits because they are unable to work, a number driven up by injuries in the coal mines, like crushed spines and black lung disease. “We have deficits here already with a lack of jobs, a lack of opportunities and being in a rural community,” Paterino said. “But what you don’t have other places that we do have is a camaraderie to help one another, neighbor helping neighbor.” “We stick together here.” Down to the last box The pallets of food were starting to shrink, and the end of the line still wasn’t in sight at Likens’ food pantry in Dunlow. He looked on nervously and tried to formulate a plan B to make sure everyone who came got something to eat. Inside his warehouse, he had some pre-packed bags for school kids he could hand out if needed. When the last of about 200 vehicles had passed through around 1 p.m., Likens was left with eight half-gallon jugs of milk, two bags of potatoes, four bags of carrots, one carton of eggs, two bags of apples and a sizable amount of sliced Swiss cheese. He’d just made it. Likens finally sat down to rest his leg, which was damaged a decade ago by bone cancer, and volunteers started moving the empty pallets and boxes inside. Then one more car pulled through. It was a worn van driven by an elderly man with a bandage around his arm from blood work and a woman with a young child in the back. A Bible sat on the dash. “You got any food left?” the man shouted from his car window. They were coming from a doctor’s appointment and weren’t able to arrive earlier, he told Likens. Likens headed back inside to see what he could round up for one last household to feed that day. “We make sure everyone gets something.”

articles.title: Democrats say they'll make life affordable. Your wallet may disagree
articles.summary: Democrats are pushing affordability as their 2026 message, but a financial advisor asks whether subsidies actually lower costs or just shift the bill.
articles.body: Democrats have discovered a wonderful new word for the 2026 elections coming to primetime. Affordability. Healthcare needs to be more affordable. SCHUMER PREACHES AFFORDABILITY IN DEM MIDTERM PITCH WHILE SABOTAGING GOP FIXES FOR SOARING COSTS Housing needs to be more affordable. Childcare needs to be more affordable. Energy needs to be more affordable. Groceries need to be more affordable. Who could possibly disagree? Certainly not me. LET SOCIALISTS ROB FROM THE RICH 100% AND YOU STILL WON’T BE ABLE TO PAY THE BILLS But as a financial advisor, I have one question whenever somebody tells me they're making something more affordable. Did you actually lower the cost, or did you just find somebody else to pay the bill? Because those are two very different things. TAX AND SPEND GOT A MARKETING MAKEOVER Democrats have made affordability a centerpiece of their 2026 economic message. LIZ PEEK: DEMOCRATS’ AFFORDABILITY SCAM COLLAPSES IN STATES THEY ACTUALLY RUN Among the ideas being discussed by progressive Democrats are $1 trillion toward new housing supply, government-produced prescription drugs, federal utility-rate standards and limits on what families pay for childcare. Other Democrats are pushing expanded healthcare subsidies and additional government assistance for families. Some proposals could attack legitimate underlying problems. Cutting zoning and permitting restrictions to build more housing, for example, could actually increase supply. I'm all for finding ways to make America build again. AMERICA’S BROKEN PERMITTING SYSTEM IS QUIETLY RAISING YOUR COST OF LIVING But too much of the affordability conversation still follows an old formula. Something costs too much. Have government pay more of it. We've seen this movie before. We used to call it tax and spend. Now we call it affordability. SOMEBODY ALWAYS PAYS Imagine your health insurance costs $20,000 a year. Government gives you an $8,000 subsidy. Your personal bill falls to $12,000. Fantastic. But healthcare didn't suddenly cost $12,000. It still cost $20,000. We simply changed who wrote part of the check. The same principle applies to childcare subsidies, housing assistance and countless tax credits. Government money isn't created by a magical ATM underneath the Capitol. It ultimately comes from taxes, borrowing or shifting resources from somewhere else. PUT IT ON THE NATIONAL CREDIT CARD This would bother me less if the federal government were swimming in excess cash. It isn't. The United States continues running enormous annual deficits while carrying a federal debt measured in the tens of trillions of dollars. Imagine a family earning $100,000 annually but spending $130,000. They're already buried in debt. Then Dad walks into the kitchen and announces: "Great news. I just made groceries more affordable." How? He put them on another credit card. Nobody would call that an affordability plan. They'd call Ted Jenkin for a financial reality check. Yet Democrats and frankly, Republicans when it suits them regularly embrace government benefits without spending nearly enough time discussing the ultimate bill. DON'T SUBSIDIZE THE PROBLEM. FIX IT. Here's the affordability agenda I'd rather hear debated. Why does America have a housing shortage? Why does it take so long and cost so much to build? Why are healthcare prices nearly impossible for consumers to understand? Why aren't there enough doctors, nurses and childcare providers? Why can't we produce and transmit more energy faster? Those are cost questions. And solving them means attacking supply, competition, regulation and productivity and not merely subsidizing demand. If we have 100 families fighting over 80 houses, giving everybody a bigger government check doesn't magically create another 20 houses. FOLLOW THE MONEY Democrats say their affordability agenda would lower costs for working families, and some of their proposals deserve a legitimate debate. But Americans should apply one simple test to every promise: Did you make it cheaper, or did you make somebody else pay for it? Because I suspect we're entering another era when government spending will increasingly be sold as the solution to the cost of living. The terminology has changed. The sales pitch is better. The algorithms repeat the message. But Americans have seen this movie before. At least I have. Tax. Spend. Subsidize. Repeat. Just don't call it that anymore. Call it affordability.
